readings.c2s3:
¶
'''unmannerly''' (un-man′ėr-li), ''a.'' '''1.''' Not mannerly; wanting in manners; not having good manners; rude in behavior; ill-bred; uncivil.
{{smaller block|<poem>I were ''unmannerly'' to take you out
And not to kiss you.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', Hen. VIII., i. 4. 95.}}
Depart, or I shall be something ''unmannerly'' with you.
{{right|''Beau. and Fl.'', King and No King, iii. 3.}}}}
'''2.''' Not according to good manners: as, an ''unmannerly'' jest. ='''Syn.''' {{smaller|See list under ''uncivil''.}}

'''unmannerly†''' (un-man′ėr-li), ''adv.'' With ill manners; uncivilly; rudely.
{{smaller block|<poem>Forgive me
If I have used myself ''unmannerly''.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', Hen. VIII., iii. 1. 176.}}}}

'''unmantle''' (un-man′tl), ''v. t.'' [< ''un-''<sup>2</sup> + ''mantle''.] To deprive of a mantle; uncover.
{{smaller block|They ''unmantled'' him of a new Plush Cloke.
{{right|''Howell'', Letters, I. i. 17.}}}}

'''unmanufactured''' (un-man-ū-fak′tụ̄rd), ''a.'' '''1.''' Not made up; still in its natural state, or only partly prepared for use: thus, fiber is ''unmanufactured'' before it is made into thread; thread is ''unmanufactured'' before it is woven into cloth. —'''2.''' Not simulated: as, ''unmanufactured'' grief. [Colloq.]

'''unmanured''' (un-mạ-nūrd′), ''a.'' '''1†.''' Untilled; uncultivated. ''Spenser.''
readings.c3s1:
'''2.''' Not manured; not enriched by manure.
{{smaller block|It is one thing to set forth what ground lieth ''unmanured'', and another thing to correct ill husbandry in that which is manured.
{{right|''Bacon'', Advancement of Learning, ii. 117.}}}}

'''unmarked''' (un-märkt′), ''a.'' '''1.''' Not marked; having no mark: as, the ''unmarked'' (south-pointing) pole of a magnet.—'''2.''' Unobserved; not regarded; undistinguished; not noted.
{{smaller block|<poem>He mix’d, ''unmark’d'', among the busy throng.</poem>
{{right|''Dryden'', All for Love, iv.}}}}

'''unmarketable''' (un-mär′ket-a̤-bl), ''a.'' Not fit for the market; not salable; of no merely pecuniary value.
{{smaller block|That paltry stone brought home to her some thought, true, spiritual, ''unmarketable.'' {{right|''Kingsley'', Hypatia, xix.}}}}

'''unmarred''' (un-märd′), ''a.'' [< ME. ''unmerred;'' < ''un-''<sup>1</sup> + ''marred.''] Not marred or injured.

'''unmarriable†''' (un-mar′i-a̤-bl), ''a.'' Not marriageable. ''Milton'', Divorce, ii. 15.

'''unmarriageable''' (un-mar′āj-a̤-bl), ''a.'' Not fit to be married; too young for marriage.

'''unmarriageableness''' (un-mar′āj-a̤-bl-nes), ''n.'' The state of being unmarriageable.

'''unmarried''' (un-mar′id), ''a.'' Not married; single: as, an ''unmarried'' woman or man. {{smaller|Commonly the word implies that the person to whom it is applied has never been married; but it may be used of a widow or widower, and possibly of a divorced person.}}
{{smaller block|<poem>That die ''unmarried'', ere they can behold
Bright Phœbus in his strength.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', W. T., iv. 4. 123.}}}}

'''unmarry''' (un-mar′i), ''v. t.'' [< ''un-''<sup>2</sup> + ''marry''<sup>1</sup>.] To divorce; dissolve the marriage contract of. [Rare.]
readings.c3s2:
¶
{{smaller block|A law . . . giving permission to ''unmarry'' a wife, and marry a lust.
{{right|''Milton'', Divorce.}}}}

'''unmartyr''' (un-mär′tėr), ''v. t.'' [< ''un-''<sup>2</sup> + ''martyr'', ''n.''] To degrade from the standing or dignity of a martyr. [Rare.]
{{smaller block|Scotus . . . was made a martyr after his death, . . . but since Baronius has ''unmartyred'' him.
{{right|''Fuller'', Ch. Hist., II. iv. 36.}}}}

'''unmasculate†''' (un-mas′kū-lāt), ''v. t.'' [< ''un-''<sup>2</sup> + ''masculate.''] To emasculate.
{{smaller block|The sins of the south ''unmasculate'' northern bodies.
{{right|''Fuller'', Holy War (1639), p. 225.}}}}

'''unmasculine''' (un-mas′kū-lin), ''a.'' Not masculine or manly. ''Milton.''

'''unmask''' (un-mȧsk′), ''v.'' [< ''un-''<sup>2</sup> + ''mask''<sup>3</sup>.] '''I.''' ''trans.'' To strip of a mask or of any disguise; lay open what is concealed; bring to light.
{{smaller block|I am ''unmasked'', unspirited, undone.
{{right|''B. Jonson'', Volpone, iii. 6.}}}}

'''II.''' ''intrans.'' To put off or lay aside a mask.
{{smaller block|My husband bids me; now I will ''unmask.''
{{right|''Shak.'', M. for M., v. 1. 206.}}}}

'''unmasked''' (un-mȧskt′), ''a.'' Not masked.

'''unmasker''' (un-mȧs′kėr), ''n.'' One who unmasks.

'''unmasterable''' (un-mȧs′tėr-a̤-bl), ''a.'' [< ''un-''<sup>2</sup> + ''master''<sup>1</sup> + ''-able.''] That cannot be mastered or subdued. ''Sir T. Browne'', Vulg. Err., iv. 2. [Rare.]

'''unmastered''' (un-mȧs′tėrd), ''a.'' '''1.''' Not subdued; not conquered.—'''2.''' Not conquerable.
{{smaller block|He cannot his ''unmaster’d'' grief sustain. {{right|''Dryden.''}}}}

'''unmatchable''' (un-mach′a-bl), ''a.'' That cannot be matched; not to be equaled; unparalleled.
readings.c3s3:
¶
{{smaller block|Most radiant, exquisite, and ''unmatchable'' beauty.
{{right|''Shak.'', T. N., i. 5. 181.}}}}

'''unmatchableness''' (un-mach′a-bl-nes), ''n.'' The character of being unmatchable; matchlessness.
{{smaller block|The presumption of his ''unmatchablenesse.''
{{right|''Bp. Hall'', Epistles, iv. 2. (''Davies.'')}}}}

'''unmatched''' (un-macht′), ''a.'' Matchless; having no match or equal.
{{smaller block|<poem>Beauty! O, it is
An ''unmatch’d'' blessing or a horrid curse.</poem>
{{right|''Ford'', Broken Heart, ii. 1.}}}}

'''unmatchedness''' (un-mach′ed-nes), ''n.'' The state of being unmatched; incomparableness. [Rare.]
{{smaller block|His clear ''unmatchedness'' in all manners of learning.
{{right|''Chapman'', Iliad, Pref.}}}}

'''unmated''' (un-mā′ted), ''a.'' Not mated; not paired.

'''unmaterial''' (un-mạ̄-tē′ri-ạl), ''a.'' Not material.
{{smaller block|The ''unmaterial'' fruits of shades. ''Daniel'', Musophilus.}}

'''unmaterialized''' (un-mạ̄-tē′ri-ạl-īzd), ''a.'' Not in bodily shape; not having become an actual fact: as, his schemes were ''unmaterialized.''

'''unmateriate†''' (un-mạ̄-tē′ri-āt), ''a.'' Not materiate.

<noinclude><pagequality level="1" user="transcriber" />{{RunningHeader|unlute|6628|unmateriate}}</noinclude>{{smaller block|Upon the ''unluting'' the vessel, it infected the room with a scarce supportable stink. {{right|''Boyle'', Works, I. 483.}}}}

'''unmade''' (un-mād′), ''a.'' [< ME. ''unmad'', *''unmaked''; < ''un-''<sup>1</sup> + ''made''<sup>1</sup>.] '''1.''' Deprived of form or qualities.—'''2.''' Not made; not yet formed.
{{smaller block|Taking the measure of an ''unmade'' grave. {{right|''Shak.'', R. and J., iii. 3. 70.}}}}
Used with ''up'': not made up; not worked into shape; not manufactured: as, ''unmade-up'' materials; an ''unmade-up'' dress.

'''unmagistrate''' (un-maj′is-trāt), ''v. t.'' [< ''un-''<sup>2</sup> + ''magistrate''.] To degrade from or deprive of the office and authority of a magistrate. ''Milton.'' [Rare.]

'''unmaiden''' (un-mā′dn), ''v. t.'' [< ''un-''<sup>2</sup> + ''maiden''.] To ravish; deflower. [Rare.]
{{smaller block|He ''unmaidened'' his sister Juno. {{right|''Urquhart'', tr. of Rabelais, iii. 12. (''Davies.'')}}}}

'''unmaidenly''' (un-mā′dn-li), ''a.'' Not befitting a maiden.
{{smaller block|The wanton gesticulations of a virgin in a wild assembly of gallants warmed with wine could be no other than riggish and ''unmaidenly''. {{right|''Bp. Hall'', Contemplations, John Baptist Beheaded.}}}}

'''unmailable''' (un-mā′lạ-bl), ''a.'' That may not be mailed: applied to matter which, by law, regulation, or treaty stipulation, is excluded from the mails, or which, by reason of illegible, incorrect, or insufficient address, cannot be forwarded to its destination. ''Glossary of U. S. Postal Terms.''

'''unmaimed''' (un-māmd′), ''a.'' Not maimed; not disabled in any limb; complete in all the parts; unmutilated; entire.
{{smaller block|It is the first grand duty of an interpreter to give his author entire and ''unmaimed.''{{right|''Pope'', Iliad, Pref.}}}}

'''unmakable''' (un-mā′ka̤-bl), ''a.'' That cannot be made.
{{smaller block|''Unmakable'' by any but a divine power.{{right|''N. Grew.''}}}}

'''unmake''' (un-māk′), ''v. t.'' [< ''un-''<sup>2</sup> + ''make''<sup>1</sup>.] '''1.''' To destroy the essential form and qualities of; cause to cease to exist; annihilate; uncreate; annul, reverse, or essentially change the nature or office of.
{{smaller block|God when he makes the prophet, does not ''unmake'' the man.{{right|''Locke.''}}
God does not make or ''unmake'' things to try experiments.{{right|''T. Burnet.''}}
Power to make emperours, and to ''vnmake'' them againe.{{right|''Jewell'', A Replie unto M. Hardinge, p. 418. (''Encyc. Dict.'')}}
Three observers, separately, on distinct occasions were in some way immediately aware when an electro-magnet was secretly “made” and “''unmade.''”{{right|''Proc. Soc. Psych. Research'', I. 236.}}}}
'''2.''' To leave unmade, unformed, uncreated, or unfashioned. [Rare.]
{{smaller block|<poem>May make, ''unmake'', do what she list.</poem>{{right|''Shak.'', Othello, ii. 3. 352.}}}}

'''unmaking''' (un-mā′king), ''n.'' The act or process of destroying; destruction; undoing; also, that which unmakes.
{{smaller block|A wife may be the making or the ''unmaking'' of the best of men.{{right|''Smiles'', Character, p. 326.}}}}

'''unmalleability''' (un-mal″ē-a̤-bil′i-ti), ''n.'' The property or state of being unmalleable.

'''unmalleable''' (un-mal′ē-a̤-bl), ''a.'' Not malleable; not capable of being extended by rolling or hammering, as a metal; hence, not capable of being shaped by outside influence; unyielding.

{{smaller block|“I do believe thee,” said the Sub-Prior; “I do believe that thine [i. e., thy mind] is indeed metal ''unmalleable'' by force.”
{{right|''Scott'', Monastery, xxxi.}}}}

'''unman''' (un-man′), ''v. t.''; pret. and pp. ''unmanned'', ppr. ''unmanning''. [< ''un-''<sup>2</sup> + ''man''.] '''1.''' To deprive of the character or qualities of a human being, as reason, etc.

{{smaller block|''Unman'' not, therefore, thyself by a bestial transformation.
{{right|''Sir T. Browne'', Christ. Mor., iii. 14.}}}}

'''2.''' To emasculate; deprive of virility.—'''3.''' To deprive of the courage and fortitude of a man; break or reduce into irresolution; dishearten; deject; make womanish.

{{smaller block|Such was his fortitude, that not even the severest trials could ''unman'' him.
{{right|''Latimer'', Life and Writings, p. xl.}}
Having made up my mind to hope no more, I got rid of a great deal of that terror which ''unmanned'' me at first.
{{right|''Poe'', Tales, I. 172.}}}}

'''4.''' To deprive of men: as, to ''unman'' a ship or town.

{{smaller block|[The daughters of Danaus were] turn’d out to Sea in a Ship ''unmann’d''.
{{right|''Milton'', Hist. Eng., i.}}}}

'''unmanacle''' (un-man′a-kl), ''v. t.'' [< ''un-''<sup>2</sup> + ''manacle''.] To release from or as from manacles; set free. ''Tennyson'', Two Voices. erned, or directed; not controlled. Hence

'''unmanageableness''' (un-man′āj-a̤-bl-nes), ''n.'' The character or state of being unmanageable.

'''unmanageably''' (un-man′āj-a̤-bli), ''adv.'' In an unmanageable manner; uncontrollably; so as to be unmanageable.
{{smaller block|Our eyes are sensitive only to ''unmanageably'' short waves.
{{right|''Nature'', XLII. 172.}}
Her hair was snow-white and ''unmanageably'' coarse.
{{right|''L. Wallace'', Ben-Hur, p. 484.}}}}

'''unmanaged''' (un-man′ājd), ''a.'' Not controlled; not restrained; specifically, not broken in, as a horse; not trained, in general.
{{smaller block|Like colts or ''unmanaged'' horses.
{{right|''Jer. Taylor'', Holy Living.}}
An unguided force, and ''unmanaged'' virtue.
{{right|''Felton'', Dissertation on Reading the Classicks.}}}}

'''unmanhood†''' (un-man′hu̇d), ''n.'' [< ME. ''unmanhode''; < ''un-''<sup>1</sup> + ''manhood''.] An unmanly or cowardly act.
{{smaller block|<poem>To slen hymself myghte he nat wynne
But bothe doon ''unmanhode'' and a synne.</poem>
{{right|''Chaucer'', Troilus, i. 824.}}}}

'''unmanlike''' (un-man′līk), ''a.'' Not manlike. {{smaller|(''a'') Unlike man in form or appearance. (''b'') Unbecoming a man as a member of the human race; inhuman; brutal.}}
{{smaller block|It is strange to see the ''unmanlike'' cruelty of mankind.
{{right|''Sir P. Sidney'', Arcadia, i.}}}}
{{smaller|(''c'') Unsuitable to a man, as opposed to a woman or child; effeminate; childish.}}
{{smaller block|By the greatness of the cry, it was the voice of a man; though it was a very ''unmanlike'' voice, so to cry.
{{right|''Sir P. Sidney.''}}}}

{{smaller block|This is ''unmanlike'', to build upon such slight airy conjectures.
{{right|''Jer. Taylor'', Works (ed. 1835), II. 392.}}}}

'''unmanliness''' (un-man′li-nes), ''n.'' The character of being unmanly; effeminacy.
{{smaller block|You and yours make piety a synonym for ''unmanliness.''
{{right|''Kingsley'', Yeast, ii.}}}}

'''unmanly''' (un-man′li), ''a.'' Not manly. {{smaller|(''a'') Not having the qualities or attributes of a man, as opposed to a woman or child; not having the strength, vigor, robustness, fortitude, or courage of a man; soft; weak; effeminate; womanish; childish: as, a poor-spirited, ''unmanly'' wretch. (''b'') Unbecoming in a man; unworthy of a man; cowardly: as, ''unmanly'' fears.}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Live, live, my matchless son,
Blest in thy father’s blessings; much more blest
In thine own vertues; let me dew thy cheeks
With my ''unmanly'' tears.</poem>
{{right|''Beau. and Fl.'', Laws of Candy, v.}}}}

'''unmanned''' (un-mand′), ''p. a.'' Not tamed; not yet familiar with man: a term in falconry.
{{smaller block|<poem>No colt is so unbroken,
Or hawk yet half so haggard or ''unmanned!''</poem>
{{right|''B. Jonson'', Sad Shepherd, iii. 2.}}
<poem>Come, civil night, . . .
Hood my ''unmann’d'' blood, bating in my cheeks,
With thy black mantle.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', R. and J., iii. 2. 14.}}}}

'''unmannered''' (un-man′ėrd), ''a.'' Uncivil; rude; mannerless.
{{smaller block|You have a slanderous . . . tongue, ''unmanner’d'' lord.
{{right|''B. Jonson'', Catiline’s Conspiracy, ii. 3.}}}}

'''unmannerliness''' (un-man′ėr-li-nes), ''n.'' The state or character of being unmannerly; want of good manners; breach of civility; rudeness of behavior.
